meta-description: Recently, I had the opportunity to go through the Amazon SDE interview loop, and I genuinely enjoyed how much the process challenged me.

It was a 4-round loop covering DSA problem solving, Low-Level Design/System Design, and Amazon Leadership Principles.

Two rounds focused on DSA questions in the LeetCode medium to medium-hard range, with patterns similar to Number of Islands and Search in Rotated Sorted Array.

One thing became clear quickly 😅 getting to a working solution is only the beginning.
Why this approach? Can you optimize it? What is the time and space complexity? What edge case could break it? What happens if the constraints change?

My earlier Microsoft interview experience taught me to clarify requirements, think aloud, discuss tradeoffs, and test edge cases instead of rushing straight into code. That definitely helped me approach this loop with more structure and confidence.

The Low-Level Design round was equally interesting. I had to take a real-world problem, identify the core objects and responsibilities, think through component relationships, extensibility, edge cases, and explain the tradeoffs behind my design decisions.

The Leadership Principles round went deep too. Ownership, Dive Deep, Deliver Results, ambiguity, mistakes, and decision making all came up through examples from my own work.

Amazon also taught me that a STAR story is never fully finished 😂
“Why?”
“What exactly did YOU do?”
“What would you do differently?”
…and suddenly you are five follow-up questions deeper.

I was informed that I successfully cleared the interview process, but the role unfortunately could not move forward because of headcount constraints. It was disappointing, but I’m grateful for the experience and the confidence it gave me.

A big thank you to the Amazon recruiting team, and the interviewers for a thoughtful and challenging experience.

Recently, I had the opportunity to go through the Amazon SDE interview loop, and I genuinely enjoyed how much the process challenged me.

It was a 4-round loop covering DSA problem solving, Low-Level Design/System Design, and Amazon Leadership Principles.

Two rounds focused on DSA questions in the LeetCode medium to medium-hard range, with patterns similar to Number of Islands and Search in Rotated Sorted Array.

One thing became clear quickly 😅 getting to a working solution is only the beginning.
Why this approach? Can you optimize it? What is the time and space complexity? What edge case could break it? What happens if the constraints change?

My earlier Microsoft interview experience taught me to clarify requirements, think aloud, discuss tradeoffs, and test edge cases instead of rushing straight into code. That definitely helped me approach this loop with more structure and confidence.

The Low-Level Design round was equally interesting. I had to take a real-world problem, identify the core objects and responsibilities, think through component relationships, extensibility, edge cases, and explain the tradeoffs behind my design decisions.

The Leadership Principles round went deep too. Ownership, Dive Deep, Deliver Results, ambiguity, mistakes, and decision making all came up through examples from my own work.

Amazon also taught me that a STAR story is never fully finished 😂
“Why?”
“What exactly did YOU do?”
“What would you do differently?”
…and suddenly you are five follow-up questions deeper.

I was informed that I successfully cleared the interview process, but the role unfortunately could not move forward because of headcount constraints. It was disappointing, but I’m grateful for the experience and the confidence it gave me.

A big thank you to the Amazon recruiting team, and the interviewers for a thoughtful and challenging experience.

    🚀 Amazon Interview Experience 2026 | SDE Role

    After getting rejected by[Amazon](https://www.linkedin.com/company/amazon?trk=public_post-text) 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐫 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔, I got another opportunity to interview with Amazon, this time through [VARITE INC](https://www.linkedin.com/company/varite?trk=public_post-text).

    Interestingly, this time 𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝟏 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧.

    The questions looked fairly straightforward at first, but became tricky if you started thinking in the wrong direction. Unfortunately, I was rejected in Round 1, but the experience gave me a clear picture of the areas I still need to work on, especially 𝐋𝐋𝐃, 𝐇𝐋𝐃, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧.

    🔹 𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝟏 - 𝟐𝟖𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

    💻 𝐃𝐒𝐀 - 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐓𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠

    Given a nested parent-child JSON structure, remove nodes with "null" data and no valid descendants. Parents that become empty after pruning should also be removed.

    𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐬: Recursion, DFS, Tree Traversal, Object Manipulation.

    🏗️ 𝐇𝐋𝐃 - 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦

    Design a locker network accessible across multiple geographical locations.

    Discussed:
• System architecture
• Locker allocation & availability
• Scalability
• User access
• Distributed-system trade-offs

    🤝 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐬

    Two LP questions focused on past experiences, ownership, decision-making, and problem-solving.

    🔑 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬

    • Don't overcomplicate straightforward DSA problems.
• System Design requires structured thinking and clear trade-offs.
• I need to strengthen my LLD & HLD fundamentals.
• Rejections can provide valuable feedback about where to improve.

    Amazon didn't work out this time either, but every interview brings a little more clarity.

    𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠. 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠. 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠. 🚀

    💼 [Amazon](https://www.linkedin.com/company/amazon?trk=public_post-text)SDE2 Interview – Round 2 Experience

    My Round 2 at Amazon shifted from pure DSA to problem-solving + system thinking, with a strong focus on how you reason.

    🧠 Coding / Design Problem

    The core problem was based on an N-ary Tree:

    ➡️ Given a list of nodes in an N-ary tree and a level L, return all nodes present at that level.

    That part was straightforward using level-order traversal.
🔗[https://lnkd.in/ghgfxPPz](https://lnkd.in/ghgfxPPz?trk=public_post-text)🔍 Follow-up (Where it got interesting)

    Now assume:
• Nodes can be added or removed dynamically
• You must return the count of nodes at any level in O(1) time

    This pushed the discussion towards:
• Pre-computing & maintaining level-wise counts
• Updating counts efficiently on insert/delete
• Trading a bit of space for constant-time queries
A great test of data structure design under changing constraints, not just coding.
🔗[https://lnkd.in/g--NmUZc](https://lnkd.in/g--NmUZc?trk=public_post-text)⭐ Leadership Principles Covered

    The interviewer clearly evaluated solutions through Amazon’s LP lens:

    1️⃣ Learn & Be Curious
• Exploring multiple approaches
• Asking clarifying questions
• Willingness to optimize beyond the obvious solution

    2️⃣ Deliver Results
• Driving the solution to completion
• Handling edge cases
• Making sure the final approach actually meets the stated time complexity

    🎯 Takeaway

    Amazon interviews are less about knowing a trick and more about:
• How deeply you understand fundamentals
• How you adapt when constraints change
• How well you balance correctness, performance, and clarity

    Solid round. Great learning experience.

    If you’re preparing for Amazon or similar product companies — think beyond the first solution. The follow-ups matter.
